In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the hot phase of IGM is a major source of fuel for low-excitation radio galaxies, but that the fuel for the more powerful radio sources is more likely to be in the form of cold gas, possibly in a cooling flow.
the accretion rate of the hot gas is the most likely cause of the radio-loudest sources, while the accretion of colder material is the most likely explanation for the less powerful radio galaxies.
the hot IGM is the fuel for radio-quiet active galaxies and for low-power radio galaxies, while for more powerful radio sources the cold phase of the ICM is the fuel.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the hot and cold phases of the IGM play different roles for the accretion and evolution of radio-loud AGNs.
radio-loud AGN are powered by a mixture of hot and cold accretion flows, and that the hot phase of radio galaxies is heated by jets and/or shocks, rather than by accretion.
the accretion of gas from the hot IGM is the main energy source of the low-excitation sources, while accretion from the cold gas is the energy source of the high-excitation radio galaxies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
accretion onto black holes in radio-loud AGNs is a complex, multi-phase process that depends on the environment and the properties of the host galaxy.

the hot phase of gas in the IGM is an efficient fuel source for the radio-loud population of active galaxies, and the accretion of this phase is likely the dominant mode of fueling for the low-power radio galaxy population.
radio galaxies are a very heterogeneous class of objects, and that the properties of the hot phase in their environments may be very different from one source to another.
